title: Thank the freed slave
hookLine: Epictetus, lame and once enslaved, taught an emperor through a book

lines: A SLAVE IN NERO'S ROME, WITH A LIMP.
cards: Emperors had well-known teachers: senators, celebrated scholars with big houses. This one's favorite reading came from somewhere else. A slave in Nero's Rome, walking with a limp.
He never writes a book. He's eventually freed, teaches in Rome, is driven out of the city along with the other philosophers, and opens a school in a provincial town in Greece.
And an emperor of Rome ends up reading his words, and thanks the friend who shared them. Three days of thanks begin here.

teach.b: First, his name. Epiktētos is an ordinary Greek word meaning acquired, and some readers hear in it a slave's name: something bought. Nobody knows what his parents called him.

Tradition says his owner was Epaphroditus, a freedman who served Nero. In the Discourses, Epictetus remembers his teacher Musonius Rufus testing him: what will you do when your master treats you badly?
Second, his limp. Ancient writers didn't agree on how it happened. One story, preserved by Origen, says a master twisted his leg until it broke, while Epictetus calmly warned him it would.
Another says it was illness. Nobody knows for sure. What is clear: the man who taught that lameness hinders the leg, not the will, was speaking from his own body.
Third, the book he didn't write. Epictetus wrote nothing.
His student Arrian took down his words as closely as he could, as reminders for himself, and in the letter at the front of the Discourses says the notes reached the public without his knowledge.
Those notes, and the little Handbook, are nearly all we have of him. Fourth, the emperor.
In the first book of the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius thanks his teacher Rusticus for many things, among them introducing him to Epictetus's teaching, sharing it from his own copy.

So the chain goes: an enslaved man, a teacher, a student's notes, a friend's copy, an emperor's notebook, and, centuries later, you. The person at the start of that chain is the one nobody would have bet on.

how: Some readers of Epictetus keep in mind that he was once enslaved and never wrote anything himself, and use that as a prompt to thank the unlikely people who have taught them.

games.q: you're Arrian, a young student, listening to Epictetus. what do you do that changes history?
o: write down his words as closely as you can
games.why: Arrian wrote them down as reminders for himself, and says they reached the public without his knowledge; without them, we'd have almost nothing of Epictetus.

practice: Think of someone who taught you something important whom you never would have expected to: a grandparent with little schooling, a coworker everyone overlooked, a child, a stranger on a bus.
Picture them clearly, and ask what they taught you, in words or just by how they lived. If thanks comes, let it go toward them.

wordCard.voice: Epiktētos, the Greek form of his name, meaning acquired: the enslaved, lame teacher whose words reached an emperor, and us. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the unlikely teacher. Some of the best lessons come from where no one was looking. See you tomorrow.
